name: Betz Limit Maximum Power
description: Gives the theoretical maximum power a wind turbine can extract from wind, per the Betz limit. It multiplies the kinetic power flux 0.5×rho×A×v³ by the ideal Betz efficiency 16/27 (about 0.593).
notes: 16/27 is the absolute upper bound; real turbines reach a lower power coefficient. Power scales with the cube of wind speed and linearly with swept area. Air density varies with altitude and temperature.

name: Wind Turbine Power Output
description: Estimates the actual electrical or mechanical power of a wind turbine. It takes the available wind kinetic power 0.5×rho×A×v³ and multiplies by the power coefficient Cp, the fraction of wind power the rotor captures.
notes: Cp cannot exceed the Betz limit of about 0.593 and typically peaks near 0.4–0.45. Output grows with the cube of wind speed, so small speed errors greatly affect results. A is the rotor swept area.

name: Wind Turbine Swept Area
description: Calculates the circular area swept by a wind turbine's rotor blades, pi×(D/2)², from the rotor diameter D. This area drives how much wind power the turbine can intercept.
notes: D is the full rotor diameter, not the radius. Result units are the square of the diameter's unit. Swept area scales with the square of diameter, so larger rotors capture disproportionately more power.

name: Wind Turbine Tip-Speed Ratio
description: Computes the tip-speed ratio (TSR), the ratio of the blade tip speed w×R to the incoming wind speed v. It is a key dimensionless parameter for matching rotor design to operating conditions.
notes: Dimensionless; w must be in rad/s. Each rotor has an optimal TSR (often 6–8 for modern three-blade turbines) that maximises the power coefficient. R is the rotor radius, not diameter.

name: Wind Power Flux Density
description: Gives the wind power available per unit area facing the flow, 0.5×rho×v³, in watts per square metre. It represents the kinetic energy flux of the wind before any turbine extraction.
notes: This is the raw resource, not extractable power; a turbine captures only a fraction (limited by Betz to 0.593). Scales with the cube of wind speed, so it is highly sensitive to v.

name: Wind Speed Log Profile (Shear)
description: Extrapolates wind speed to a target height z using the logarithmic wind profile. It scales the reference speed vr by the ratio of log-height terms ln(z/z0)/ln(zr/z0), based on surface roughness length z0.
notes: Valid for neutral atmospheric stability in the surface layer. Heights z, z0 and zr must share units and z, zr must exceed z0. Roughness length z0 characterises the terrain, not a physical height.

name: Wind Speed Power-Law Profile
description: Extrapolates wind speed to height z with the power-law profile. It multiplies the reference speed vr by (z/zr) raised to the shear exponent alpha, a simple empirical alternative to the log law.
notes: The exponent alpha (often about 0.14 over open land) depends on terrain and stability. Heights z and zr must share units; only their ratio matters. Purely empirical, so alpha should be site-calibrated.

name: Capacity Factor
description: Computes the capacity factor of a power plant: the actual energy produced divided by the energy it would produce running at rated power for the whole period, En/(Pr×t). It reflects how fully the plant is utilised.
notes: Result is a fraction between 0 and 1 (multiply by 100 for percent). Energy and power units must be consistent so Pr×t matches En's units, and t must be the same period over which En was measured.

name: Photovoltaic Array Power Output
description: Estimates the instantaneous power of a PV array. It multiplies array area A, incident irradiance G, module efficiency eta and performance ratio PR to give the AC power delivered under those conditions.
notes: eta and PR are fractions, not percentages. PR lumps together losses from temperature, wiring, inverter and soiling. Result is instantaneous power at the given irradiance, not daily energy.

name: PV Daily Energy Yield
description: Estimates the daily energy a PV system produces. It multiplies the array's rated STC power by the peak sun hours for the day and the performance ratio, Pstc×psh×PR, giving energy in kilowatt-hours.
notes: Peak sun hours is the daily irradiation expressed as equivalent hours at 1000 W/m², not clock hours of daylight. PR (a fraction) captures system losses. Multiply by days for longer periods.

name: PV Annual Energy Yield
description: Estimates yearly PV energy by scaling the daily yield Pstc×psh×PR over 365 days. It combines rated STC power, average peak sun hours per day and the performance ratio into an annual kilowatt-hour total.
notes: Assumes a constant average of peak sun hours per day; real output varies seasonally. Uses 365 days, ignoring leap years. psh is the daily average here, and PR is a fraction covering system losses.

name: PV Output After Degradation
description: Projects a PV system's power after n years of aging. Starting from the initial power P0, it applies the annual degradation rate d compounded over n years, P0×(1−d)^n.
notes: d is a per-year fraction (e.g. 0.005 for 0.5%/yr), applied as compound decay rather than linear loss. n is whole or fractional years. Excludes sudden faults; represents only gradual degradation.

name: Temperature-Corrected PV Power
description: Adjusts a PV module's rated power for cell temperature. It scales the STC power by 1+tc×(Tc−25), where tc is the temperature coefficient and 25°C is the standard reference cell temperature.
notes: The temperature coefficient tc is negative for power (per °C), so hotter cells give less output. Reference is 25°C; Tc is cell temperature, typically well above ambient in sunlight.

name: Solar Cell Fill Factor
description: Computes the fill factor of a solar cell, the ratio of maximum-power-point output Vmp×Imp to the product of open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current Voc×Isc. It measures how square the I–V curve is.
notes: Dimensionless, always between 0 and 1; typical cells are 0.7–0.85. Higher fill factor means lower internal losses. Vmp and Imp are the values at the maximum power point, not the rated maxima.

name: Solar Cell Conversion Efficiency
description: Calculates a solar cell's conversion efficiency: the maximum electrical power FF×Voc×Isc divided by the incident optical power A×G. It gives the fraction of sunlight converted to electricity.
notes: Dimensionless fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Usually evaluated at STC with G=1000 W/m². A is the cell area exposed to light; ensure A and G units are consistent with power in watts.

name: Hydroelectric Power Output
description: Estimates the electrical power of a hydroelectric plant from the flow rate Q and net head H. It combines the water's gravitational potential energy rate rho×g×Q×H with the overall efficiency eta.
notes: H is the net head after subtracting penstock and friction losses, not the gross head. eta bundles turbine, generator and hydraulic efficiencies. Result is in watts; divide by 1000 for kilowatts.

name: Hydroelectric Annual Energy
description: Estimates the annual energy of a hydro plant by multiplying its rated power by the capacity factor and the 8760 hours in a year, P×CF×8760. It reflects real utilisation over the year.
notes: Capacity factor CF (a fraction 0–1) accounts for variable flow and downtime. Uses 8760 hours, assuming a non-leap year. Keep P in kW so energy comes out in kWh.

name: Pumped-Storage Stored Energy
description: Estimates the recoverable energy of a pumped-storage reservoir. It multiplies the water's gravitational potential energy rho×g×V×H by the round-trip efficiency eta to give the deliverable energy in joules.
notes: V is the volume of water moved and H the effective head between reservoirs. eta accounts for both pumping and generating losses. Result is in joules; divide by 3.6e6 for kWh.

name: Levelized Cost of Energy (Simplified)
description: Estimates the levelized cost of energy: annualized capital cost C×crf plus annual operation and maintenance OM, divided by the annual energy produced En. It gives the average cost per kilowatt-hour.
notes: The capital recovery factor crf annualizes the up-front cost over the project life; C and OM must be in the same currency and En in the same energy unit as the result. Simplified: ignores fuel and inflation.

name: Capital Recovery Factor
description: Computes the capital recovery factor, the constant annual payment per unit of present value needed to repay a loan over n periods at discount rate i, i×(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n−1).
notes: i is a per-period fraction (e.g. 0.06 for 6%) and n the number of periods, usually years. Multiply a present capital cost by this factor to get its equivalent annual cost. Requires i greater than 0.

name: Simple Payback Period
description: Calculates the simple payback period: the capital cost C divided by the annual saving S, giving the number of years for cumulative savings to equal the initial investment.
notes: Ignores the time value of money, discounting, degradation and rising or falling savings; it is a rough screening metric. C and S must use the same currency for the result to be in years.

name: Battery Energy Capacity (Wh)
description: Converts a battery's charge capacity in amp-hours to energy in watt-hours by multiplying the nominal voltage V by the amp-hour rating Ah, V×Ah.
notes: Uses nominal voltage; actual delivered energy varies as voltage sags during discharge. This is total stored energy, not usable energy—apply a depth-of-discharge limit for the latter.

name: Battery Backup Runtime
description: Estimates how long a battery can supply a load. It takes the stored energy En, reduces it by the usable fraction DoD and inverter efficiency eta, then divides by the load power P to give runtime in hours.
notes: DoD and eta are fractions; En should be in watt-hours and P in watts so the result is hours. Assumes constant load; real runtime falls under higher loads and low temperatures.

name: Inverter Output Power
description: Computes the AC output power of an inverter as the DC input power Pdc multiplied by the inverter efficiency eta, accounting for conversion losses.
notes: eta is a fraction (e.g. 0.96), not a percentage, and typically varies with load level. The lost power (1−eta)×Pdc becomes heat, which the inverter must dissipate.

name: Incident Solar Irradiance on Tilted Surface
description: Projects direct-beam solar irradiance onto a surface using the cosine of the incidence angle. It multiplies the beam irradiance G0 by cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the sun's rays and the surface normal.
notes: theta is in radians and measured from the surface normal, so theta=0 gives full irradiance. Covers only the direct beam, ignoring diffuse and reflected components. Values beyond 90 degrees give zero or negative and are unphysical.

name: Solar Zenith Angle Cosine
description: Computes the cosine of the solar zenith angle from latitude, solar declination and hour angle, sin(lat)×sin(dec)+cos(lat)×cos(dec)×cos(H). This value sets how directly sunlight strikes a horizontal surface.
notes: All angles are in radians. The result is the cosine, ranging from 1 (sun overhead) toward 0 at the horizon; negative values mean the sun is below the horizon. Hour angle is zero at solar noon.

name: Optical Air Mass (Secant Approximation)
description: Estimates the relative optical air mass as the secant of the solar zenith angle, 1/cos(z). It gives the path length of sunlight through the atmosphere relative to the vertical (zenith) path.
notes: z is in radians; air mass equals 1 at the zenith and rises steeply near the horizon. This simple secant form breaks down above about 80 degrees, where atmospheric refraction requires corrected formulas.

name: Solar Thermal Collector Heat Output
description: Estimates the useful heat delivered by a solar thermal collector. It multiplies the collector area A, incident irradiance G and collector efficiency eta to give the thermal power in watts.
notes: eta is a fraction that depends on operating temperature and ambient conditions, not a fixed rating. Result is instantaneous thermal power; integrate over time for energy. G is irradiance on the collector plane.
